newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenians wary of EU entry, criticise Drnovsek.
newsitem.headline: Slovenians wary of EU entry, criticise Drnovsek.

text.p: Slovenians expected few dramatic changes in Sunday's general election, but farmers said on Friday they mostly feared a headlong rush to join the European Union.
The government of centrist Prime Minister Janez Drnovsek, has made EU entry one its main election campaign platforms and expects to join the Brussels club by the year 2001.
"The prices of our products are already too low," said Slavko Zarivsek, 71, who rears cows, pigs and chickens on his small farm in Smarje, 30 km (20 miles) southeast of Ljubljana.
"After joining the EU, the situation will only get worse and prices will fall even further," said Zarivsek, standing in his farmhouse cellar where he distils apple and pear schnaps.

Slovenia's mountain pastures bear a striking resemblance to the Alpine farms north of the border in Austria, where farmers have begun to feel the financial strain of nearly two years of EU membership.
Zarivsek, a World War Two veteran, said he voted for the United List of Social Democrats, the former communist party, in the last general election in 1992 and would do so again.

His neighbour, dairy farmer Franc Zajc, complained that Drnovsek's government had done little to give back the land to farmers which was nationalised when Marshal Josip Broz Tito's communist government took power in 1945.
"We have lived badly and I expect our lives will only get worse after joining the EU. They will just swallow us up," Zajc, 58, said.
He said he would vote for one of the rightist parties, who have set up an informal alliance called the "Slovenian Spring".
The alliance consists of the rightist People's Party, the Christian Democrats and centre-right Social Democrats.
All back EU membership but the People's Party led by Marjan Podobnik has called for caution over joining the EU, saying farmers livelihoods had to be protected.
Farmers and agricultural workers make up around 20 percent of the work force.
The rightist bloc is hoping to clinch a vital 50 percent of the vote, but will have difficulty ousting Drnovsek's centre-left Liberal Democrats, who currently have most support in opinion polls.
In the capital, Ljubljana, where the baroque architecture bears testimony to the rule of the Austro-Hungarian empire, voters were critical of Drnovsek's four-year term of office.
Unemployed factory worker, Djurdja Zvonarek, 42, said she had voted for Drnovsek in 1992, but described his economic policies as a disaster.
"I expect the 'Spring' parties to win. If they stick to what they have promised, they should improve our standard of living," she said.

Ibro Zare, 50, who fought in Slovenia's war of independence from former Yugoslavia in June 1991, said he would vote for his former commander, ex-defence minister Janez Jansa, who is now leader of the Social Democrats.
"Today we have nothing because of the current government, but Slovenia could be a second Switzerland," Zare said.
"We cannot go barefoot and naked into Europe. First the politicians should take care of jobs and the economy here before considering joining the EU," he said.
